How much does Poshmark take per sale?

Poshmark publishes one schedule with two rules, not a single percentage. Sales under $15.00 pay a flat $2.95 fee. Sales of $15.00 or more pay 20% of the sale price. That is a real cliff — the whole price is taxed under whichever rule applies, not just the part above $15 — and it is why "Poshmark takes 20%" is only true above the line.

The formula

commission = price < $15.00 ? $2.95 : 20% × price

payout = price − commission

Poshmark's flat buyer-paid shipping fee is not part of this at all — it funds a prepaid label and Poshmark takes no commission on it, unlike a marketplace that commissions the checkout total.

Worked example 1: Poshmark's own $50 sale

LineAmount
Sale price$50.00
Commission (20% of $50)$10.00
Payout$40.00

This is the number on Poshmark's own "How Selling Works" page: sell for $50, keep $40.

Worked example 2: a $10 item — the flat fee is a worse deal than it looks

LineAmount
Sale price$10.00
Commission (flat fee, under $15)$2.95
Payout$7.05
Effective rate29.5%

29.5%, not 20% and not "a small flat fee." The cheaper the item, the worse this gets: a $5 item pays $2.95 on a $5 sale — an effective 59% rate.

The break-even price: $14.75

Twenty percent of $14.75 is exactly $2.95. That makes $14.75 the price where the flat fee and the percent rate cost the same. Above $14.75 (and still under $15.00) the flat fee is a bargain against 20%. Below $14.75 the flat fee costs more than 20% would, and the gap widens fast as price drops — which matters most for jewelry, accessories, and other low-price closet items where $2.95 is a large share of the sale.

Worked example 3: right at the $15.00 line

Sale priceTierCommissionPayout
$14.99Flat$2.95$12.04
$15.0020%$3.00$12.00

One cent of price crossing the $15.00 line is worth four cents of payout — in the seller's favor, at the lower price. See is a lower offer worth it on Poshmark? for what this means when you are negotiating an offer or a bundle discount near the line.

Do this with your own listings

The Poshmark fee calculator runs this same arithmetic on your own sale price, item cost, and prep cost, and solves for the price you need to hit a target profit. Nothing you type leaves your browser.

Common questions

How much does Poshmark take on a $50 sale?

Poshmark's own published example: a $50 item pays 20% commission, which is $10.00, leaving a $40.00 payout. That is the standard rate for any sale of $15.00 or more.

How much does Poshmark take on a $10 sale?

$2.95 — the flat fee that applies under $15.00, regardless of how far under. On a $10 item that is a 29.5% effective rate, well above the 20% rate that applies at $15 and up.

What is the Poshmark break-even price?

$14.75. Twenty percent of $14.75 is exactly $2.95, the flat fee. Above $14.75 (and below $15) the flat fee is cheaper than 20% would be. Below $14.75 the flat fee costs more than 20% would, and the gap widens the cheaper the item gets.

No warranty. This page is free arithmetic, not legal, tax, financial, or selling advice. Rates change and are set by Poshmark, not by this site. Verify every figure against your own Poshmark payout statement before you price a listing. Is a lower offer worth it on Poshmark?

Whenever you accept a lower offer or set a bundle discount, part of that discount comes out of Poshmark's commission and part comes out of your own payout — and how the split works depends entirely on which side of $15.00 you land on.

Above $15.00: Poshmark shares in every discount

In the 20% tier, commission is 20% of whatever the buyer actually pays. Drop the price and the commission drops with it — automatically, proportionally.

LineListed at $40Offer at $35
Commission (20%)$8.00$7.00
Payout$32.00$28.00

The $5 discount only costs $4.00 in payout — Poshmark absorbed the other dollar. Any discount that keeps both prices at $15 or more works this way: you only ever absorb 80% of it.

Below $15.00: the fee is fixed, so you absorb the whole discount

The flat $2.95 fee does not move once you are under $15.00, no matter how much lower the price goes. A discount that keeps both prices under $15 comes entirely out of your own pocket.

LineListed at $12Offer at $8
Commission (flat)$2.95$2.95
Payout$9.05$5.05

The full $4 discount lands in your payout, dollar for dollar — Poshmark's cut never moves.

Crossing the line: usually a one-time break, not a penalty

It is tempting to assume crossing under $15.00 makes things worse, since it feels like leaving one tier for a "cheaper item" tier. It is the opposite: twenty percent of anything at or above $14.75 is already at least $2.95, so the flat fee is never a bigger bite than the percent rate would have been at that price. Crossing the line is a one-time reduction in commission.

LineListed at $20Offer at $14
Commission$4.00 (20%)$2.95 (flat)
Payout$16.00$11.05

The sticker discount is $6.00. The actual payout drop is $4.95 — never more than the discount, because the commission itself fell by $1.05 on the way down.

Worked example: one cent can raise your payout

The most surprising case is right at the boundary. A $15.00 sale pays 20% commission. A $14.99 sale — one cent lower — pays the flat fee instead.

Sale priceTierCommissionPayout
$15.0020%$3.00$12.00
$14.99Flat$2.95$12.04

The one-cent-lower sale pays four cents more. If a buyer's offer lands one cent under $15.00, taking it can put more in your pocket than holding firm at $15.00 — the opposite of what most sellers assume.

Do this with your own offers

The Poshmark fee calculator's offer comparison runs this same arithmetic on your own listed price and offer, and names how much of the discount came from Poshmark's cut versus your own payout. Nothing you type leaves your browser.

Common questions

Does Poshmark share in a discount I offer?

Yes, but only above $15.00. In the 20% tier, commission is 20% of whatever the buyer pays, so a $5 discount only costs you $4 — Poshmark's cut shrinks by $1 automatically. Under $15.00 the fee is a fixed $2.95 no matter the price, so any discount there comes entirely out of your own payout.

Does accepting an offer that drops below $15 cost me more?

Usually less, not more. Twenty percent of anything at or above $14.75 is at least $2.95, so switching to the flat fee is a one-time reduction in commission. A $20 listing dropping to a $14 offer loses $6 in sale price but only $4.95 in payout, because the fee itself dropped by $1.05.

Can a lower price ever pay me more?

Yes, right at the boundary. A $15.00 sale pays 20% ($3.00 commission, $12.00 payout). A $14.99 sale — one cent lower — pays the flat $2.95 fee ($12.04 payout). The one-cent-lower sale nets four cents more.

vs-poshmarks-how-it-works-page.html.text:
← Poshmark fee calculator

This calculator vs. Poshmark's own How It Works page

Poshmark states its current seller rate schedule on its own How It Works page and Help Center: a flat $2.95 fee on sales under $15, and 20% of the sale price on sales of $15 or more, with a prepaid USPS shipping label, payment processing, and seller protection already folded into that one number — no separate listing fee, no subscription, no line-item processing charge. Poshmark's own worked example is a $50 sale paying a $10.00 fee, leaving the seller $40.00. That schedule is free to check any time and is the right place to confirm what the current rate actually is.

It is worth checking, because it has moved once already. On October 3, 2024, Poshmark replaced this schedule with a 5.99%-of-order-total fee plus a flat $1–$3 tier, and added a matching Buyer Protection Fee charged to buyers. Sellers reported lower sales volume as buyers adjusted to the higher checkout total, and Poshmark reversed the change on October 24, 2024, restoring the original 20%/$2.95 split this calculator uses. Older seller guides and blog posts written during or just after that three-week window can still cite the reverted numbers — a real source of the exact kind of stale-fee confusion a page like this exists to clear up. Poshmark's own How It Works page reflects whichever schedule is current; this calculator is only as current as that page, so re-check it if a sale's numbers ever look off.

What Poshmark's own resources do not do is run the arithmetic on a decision still in front of a seller: whether $2.95 flat is actually cheaper than 20% would have been at this price, what a sale nets after the seller's own item cost and packaging, what price to set for a target profit, and whether accepting a lower offer or bundle price costs more of Poshmark's cut or more of the seller's own payout. This calculator does not try to store Poshmark's rate schedule as a lookup table that could drift out of date — it applies the two published tiers directly to whatever numbers are typed in, so it stays correct as long as the published schedule itself does.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What does Poshmark currently charge in seller fees? Poshmark's own How It Works page.
Is the flat $2.95 fee actually cheaper than 20% would be at this price? This calculator's sale section — see the worked break-even example on how much does Poshmark take per sale.
What do I actually keep after my own item and packaging cost? This calculator's sale section.
What price do I need to set to hit a target profit? This calculator's sale section (target-profit price).
Does accepting this offer or bundle price cost me more than the discount looks like? This calculator's offer comparison section — see the worked examples on is a lower offer worth it on Poshmark.

This tool needs no Poshmark account and no active listing: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs entirely in your browser, and once loaded it keeps working with the connection off. Sale prices, costs, and payouts are never uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Poshmark's own How It Works page?

Both, for different jobs. Poshmark's own How It Works page and Help Center state the current rate schedule: a flat $2.95 fee under $15, 20% of the sale price at $15 or more, with a prepaid shipping label and payment processing already included. That is the right place to confirm what the rate currently is. It does not compute the $14.75 break-even price where the flat fee equals 20%, does not show your profit after your own item and prep cost, does not solve for the price that hits a target profit, and does not check whether accepting a lower offer or bundle price actually costs more of Poshmark's cut or more of your own payout. This calculator does not try to reproduce Poshmark's rate schedule as a stored table — it applies the published tiers directly to the numbers you type, so it stays correct as long as the schedule itself does.

Does Poshmark have its own interactive fee calculator?

No. Poshmark's own materials state the schedule in prose and worked examples (a $50 item pays $10.00 and the seller keeps $40.00), but publish no what-if tool of their own for a different sale price, a different cost basis, or a lower offer.

Why does the fee schedule need double-checking at all?

Because it changed once already, recently. On October 3, 2024, Poshmark replaced the 20%/$2.95 split with a 5.99%-of-order-total-plus-$1/$2/$3 tiered fee and a matching buyer-side Buyer Protection Fee, then reversed course three weeks later on October 24, 2024 after seller backlash over reduced sales volume, restoring the original 20%/$2.95 schedule this calculator uses. Search results and older seller guides published during or shortly after that window can still cite the reverted numbers, which is exactly the kind of drift worth checking against Poshmark's own current page rather than a cached blog post.

Is this page affiliated with Poshmark?

vs-tracking-poshmark-payouts-in-a-spread.text:
← Poshmark Fee Calculator

Poshmark Fee Calculator vs. tracking payouts in a spreadsheet

A seller listing more than a few pieces usually ends up with a spreadsheet: one cell for the flat $2.95 fee, one for the 20% rate, and an IF formula to pick between them at the $15.00 line. That formula is ordinary arithmetic. What it does not do by itself is flag the $14.75 price where the two rules cost the same, or catch the moment an offer or bundle discount drops a sale from just above $15.00 to just below it — the one case where accepting less money can also mean losing more of it to fees.

What each approach actually does

A spreadsheet can reproduce the whole fee schedule: =IF(price<15,2.95,price*0.2) for commission, and price minus that for payout. Typing the formula once and copying it down handles any number of listings, and a spreadsheet keeps a running history a calculator does not.

This calculator keeps that same formula, plus the $14.75 break-even price and the offer/bundle-discount comparison, on one screen, and solves for the price needed to hit a target profit instead of a goal-seek you build yourself. A shareable link carries the whole scenario in the URL, so a number checked before listing is the same link opened again after an offer comes in.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What do I keep on this listing after fees?This calculator's payout panel, or your own IF formula — both give the same number.
Does this offer or bundle discount cost more than it looks like once fees shift?This calculator's offer comparison, not a second spreadsheet formula most sellers never write.
What price do I need to list at for a target profit?This calculator's target-profit mode, solved for you instead of goal-seeked by hand.
I want a running history across a season of listings.A spreadsheet you build yourself — it can track any number of rows over time.
Is my data uploaded anywhere?No. Everything runs in your browser; your figures stay on this device.

Common questions

Can a spreadsheet do this math instead?

Yes. The fee schedule is one IF formula — commission equals $2.95 when the sale price is under $15.00, otherwise 20% of the sale price — and payout is sale price minus commission. Anyone who can write =IF(A2<15,2.95,A2*0.2) has the core arithmetic. Building it means typing that formula once and copying it down.

What does a spreadsheet not do that this calculator does?

Surface the $14.75 break-even price and the offer-negotiation risk without a second formula. A basic IF formula answers what you keep on a listed price; it does not, on its own, show that accepting an offer or bundle discount which drops the final price from just above $15.00 to just below it can cost more in lost commission-tier savings than the discount itself, because the fee jumps from 20% of the higher price straight to a flat $2.95 that is nearly as large. This calculator runs that comparison in one view and solves for the sale price needed to hit a target profit, instead of a goal-seek you set up yourself.

Is a spreadsheet ever the better choice?

Yes, when your situation has a wrinkle this calculator does not model — tracking dozens of listings across a season, reconciling against Poshmark's own payout CSV, or a bulk-discount promotion this tool's inputs cannot represent. A spreadsheet you build yourself can represent any rule you can describe and keep a running history. This calculator trades that flexibility for a form that already has the right cliff, break-even, and offer comparison wired in for a single sale.

Is my data uploaded anywhere?

No. The calculator runs entirely in your browser. A shareable link carries your numbers in the URL itself rather than sending them to a server, and the optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never your prices or costs.

This page names no specific product — it compares against the generic method of tracking these payouts in a spreadsheet, not a competing calculator. Open the Poshmark Fee Calculator, or see how much does Poshmark take per sale for the worked $14.75 break-even example.
